objectives: Use a dummy node so the head has a node before it like every other node.
Delete nodes while walking, keeping a reference to the node before.
Keep relinking code simple enough to check by drawing arrows.

sections.heading: Intuition: give the head a node before it
paragraphs: To remove a node, you change the next of the node before it. Every node has one, except the head. That's why list code is full of "if we're removing the head" special cases.
A dummy node fixes that. Put an extra node in front of the head. Now every real node, including the first, has a node before it. When you're done, the answer is dummy.next.

callout.text: When the head itself might change, start with a dummy node in front of it and return dummy.next.

diagram.description: A dummy node D in front of 9 and 1. The 9 can be removed by changing the dummy's next.

sections.heading: Baseline: handle the head separately
paragraphs: Without a dummy, first remove matching nodes from the front by moving head forward, then walk the rest with a prev reference. It works, but it's two loops that must agree, and bugs hide in the handoff between them.

sections.heading: Worked example: remove every node above a limit
paragraphs: Start prev at the dummy. While prev.next exists: if prev.next should go, skip it by setting prev.next = prev.next.next, and don't move prev. Otherwise move prev forward.
Not moving prev after a removal matters: the node that just became prev.next hasn't been checked. The edge case removes the first two nodes, which only works cleanly because of the dummy.

sections.heading: Complexity and cautions
paragraphs: Walking with prev and a dummy node is O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.
Draw the arrows before and after each operation on paper. If the drawing is right and each line of code matches one arrow change, the code is right.

sections.heading: Before you finish
paragraphs: Try to answer each question before opening it.

checks.prompt: Why return dummy.next instead of head?
checks.answer: The original head may have been removed. dummy.next is always the current first node.

checks.prompt: Why doesn't prev move after a removal?
checks.answer: The node that just became prev.next hasn't been checked yet.

checks.prompt: What special case does the dummy remove?
checks.answer: Removing or changing the first node, which otherwise has no node before it.
